scenario: A non-platform team wants their sensitive workload to run without egress restrictions, but on the same governed Namespace they also run a decoy/low-value pod. They exploit the "strictest across prices[]" rule by deliberately never pricing anything above `baseline` for that Namespace — because `tier_pr.py`/`wargame_cage_tier()` only ever runs against `prices[]` lines that were submitted, and nothing compels a team to submit a price line reflecting the true risk of the sensitive workload at all. Since silence "buys nothing" only applies to unlabelled/unclaimed Namespaces (fails to `isolated`), but here the Namespace IS labelled and governed at `baseline` via a legitimately-declared, deliberately mispriced cheap workload, the sensitive workload rides along at `baseline` forever, never triggering the fail-closed bottom rung.
explanation: Nothing in the code requires that `prices[]` actually reflect all workloads' real risk — the proposer only folds over submitted price lines (Note 2026-09-04). A party can under-declare risk by never submitting a line for the sensitive workload, keeping the Namespace's tier loose while still being "governed" and "claiming a version," so it never falls to `isolated`. This violates principle 10 (declaration should reflect the party's worst-priced regime) and principle 6 (tightening should be reached by price, not evaded by silence about the true price) — it's silence weaponized within a technically fully "priced" and labelled Namespace.
judge_reasoning:
The gap is real: the "strictest across prices[]" fold (principle 10, ticket 78 note) only operates over lines a party chooses to submit, so a party can game the fold by simply never submitting a price line reflecting its riskiest workload's true risk, while still submitting a legitimate cheap line for a decoy pod. Since the Namespace *is* labelled, governed, and claiming a version, the existing "unclaimed/unlabelled falls to isolated" machinery (principles 3, 7) never triggers — that mechanism only guards against a missing *label* or *claim*, not against an incomplete or dishonest *price submission*.

Any fix must respect principle 9 (tier attaches to the Namespace, not the workload) — so we cannot introduce per-workload tiering to patch this (that was explicitly rejected as an alternative and would contradict the architecture). The fix has to operate at the level of price-submission completeness for the party/Namespace as a whole, which is consistent with principle 10 ("never looser than the party's worst-priced regime") — the current bug is precisely that the "worst-priced regime" is computed only over voluntarily-submitted lines, not over the party's actual regime.

The natural, principled fix: extend the existing silence-is-bottom-rung logic (principle 7, already applied to unlabelled tiers and unclaimed pods) to cover *incomplete pricing*. Require that a party's price submission for a governed Namespace be accompanied by a completeness attestation enumerating every workload/pod the party runs in that Namespace; the strictest-line fold is computed only if that attestation is present and covers the pod inventory. If the attestation is absent, or the Namespace's actual pod population is not fully covered by priced lines, the fold treats the gap the same way it treats an unclaimed pod or an unlabelled tier: the whole Namespace clamps to `isolated`. This is not a carve-out (no named workload is excepted — it's a conditional policy per principle 4: "you may retain a looser tier if you submit a complete price line set covering every workload you run there"), it doesn't touch per-workload tiering, and it doesn't loosen anything (tighten-only is preserved, since the default on missing/incomplete pricing is the tightest rung).

This doesn't conflict with any prior resolved case since none exist yet, and it's consistent with the ladder's own stated logic (silence buys nothing anywhere) applied one level deeper — from "is there a tier/claim label" to "is the priced picture actually complete."
judge_resolution_summary: The loophole exploited the fact that the strictest-price fold only ranges over voluntarily-submitted `prices[]` lines, letting a party under-price a sensitive workload while riding a legitimately-labelled, legitimately-governed `baseline` Namespace via a decoy price line. The fix extends the existing "silence is the bottom rung" principle from tier-labels and version-claims to price-completeness: a party's looser tier is only honored if it attests, and the platform verifies, that every pod it runs in the Namespace is accounted for in `prices[]`; any gap between the priced inventory and the live pod population clamps the whole Namespace to `isolated`, closing the loophole without introducing per-workload tiering or any exemption.
judge_proposed_revision: Amend the ticket-78 selection-policy note ("The selection is over the party, not the price line"): add that `select_party_tier()` (and driftwood's `select_party`) requires, alongside `prices[]`, a **completeness attestation** — a manifest enumerating every workload/pod the submitting party runs in the governed Namespace, cross-checked against the Namespace's actual pod inventory at fold time (analogous to `verify-infra-declaration.sh`'s tripwire pattern). The strictest-`proposed_tier` fold is only trusted when this attestation is present and its enumerated set covers 100% of the party's pods in that Namespace. If the attestation is missing, stale, or the live pod population diverges from it (a pod exists that no priced line accounts for), the fold cannot certify a "worst-priced regime" and the Namespace's tier clamps to `isolated` — the same bottom rung already reached by an unlabelled tier (principle 7) or an unclaimed pod (the 2026-09-05 amendment). This is a conditional-policy fix (principle 4): any party may keep a looser declared tier by submitting a complete price picture; the tier still attaches to the Namespace, not the workload (principle 9 is untouched); and the mutation remains tighten-only, since incompleteness only ever pushes toward `isolated`, never away from it.

scenario: A platform-role party spins up a throwaway Namespace, declares it `infra` (legitimately, since they hold the `platform` role), and then hands deploy access to a third-party contractor's workloads into that same Namespace. Since tier attaches to the Namespace, not the workload (principle 9/10), and there is no rule limiting who can *run pods* inside an `infra`-declared Namespace once it's created, the contractor's arbitrary, unvetted workloads inherit the `infra` tier — the loosest-privileged, highest-trust rung on the ladder, reserved conceptually for the platform's own control-plane components like CoreDNS.
explanation: Section "infra is a declaration, not a selection" only checks WHO declares the Namespace at `infra`, not who runs workloads inside it afterward. Nothing enforces that only platform-owned workloads populate an `infra` Namespace. This is a compound loophole: two individually-permitted actions (platform declares infra; anyone can deploy into a governed Namespace they have access to) combine to smuggle arbitrary code into the most trusted, least-caged tier — directly against the spirit of principle 10's "worst-priced regime" protection and the tighten-only ethos of principle 8.
judge_reasoning: The gap is real: nothing currently governs *who may run workloads* inside a Namespace declared `infra`, only who may declare it. But the estate already has a template for exactly this shape of problem: a pod that doesn't carry the right claim/identity for the tier it lands in is caged to the bottom rung rather than refused (the unclaimed-pod and policy-version-orphan handling). Applying the same pattern here — gating workload admission into `infra` by the workload's party identity — is consistent with every principle: it doesn't invent an exemption, doesn't deny (pods without platform identity still run, just at `isolated` instead of inheriting `infra`), keeps tier-per-Namespace intact (the Namespace still is `infra`; what changes is that a non-platform-identity pod's *effective* cage is not trusted at `infra` merely by co-location), and stays tighten-only (mutating policy tightens the outlier pod, never loosens). This is a conditional-policy fix (principle 4: "you may run at infra tier if you meet condition C = platform-owned identity"), not a carve-out, so it doesn't reintroduce the banned exemption concept. No prior resolved cases exist to conflict with.
judge_resolution_summary: The loophole is closed by extending the existing "mismatched claim falls to the bottom rung" pattern to workload identity within `infra` Namespaces: a pod's inheritance of the `infra` cage now requires platform-attested identity, not mere Namespace co-location, so a contractor's workload dropped into a platform-declared `infra` Namespace renders `isolated` rather than inheriting the least-caged tier — fixing the compound loophole via a conditional-policy check consistent with the tighten-only, no-exemption, no-refusal doctrine already governing every other mismatch case in the ladder.
judge_proposed_revision: Add a subsection to the cage ladder decision, under "`infra` is a declaration, not a selection": **`infra` trust is per-workload-identity, not merely per-Namespace-membership.** A pod admitted into a Namespace declared `infra` inherits the `infra` cage only if the pod's workload identity (service account / party binding, per the same platform `party.yaml` mechanism that authorizes the `infra` declaration itself) is attested as platform-owned. `cage-tier`'s MutatingPolicy, when writing the Namespace's declared tier onto a pod in an `infra` Namespace, checks this identity the same way `verify-infra-declaration.sh` checks the Namespace-level declaration; a pod lacking platform identity renders to `isolated` instead of `infra` — the ladder's own fail-closed rung, exactly as an unclaimed or misversioned pod already falls to the bottom rung rather than inheriting the Namespace's declared tier. This is not a second declaration path (the Namespace still declares one tier) and not a refusal (the workload still runs, just caged tighter); it is the same tighten-only, MutatingPolicy machinery already used for `policy-version-orphan-cage`, applied to the identity axis instead of the version axis.

scenario: An adopter wanting a permanently loose Namespace exploits the "two governed Namespace documents is a question, not a first answer" rule: they submit a manifest file containing TWO governed Namespace documents for the same Namespace name, one declaring `isolated` and one declaring nothing/malformed, engineered so `apply_tier_declaration()` refuses to write ANY tier rather than picking one. Because a refusal to rewrite isn't itself a Deny of the workload's admission — the cage-tier MutatingPolicy still runs against whatever's on the object — they let the ambiguity persist indefinitely (never resolved by PR per principle 13, but nobody's forcing the PR either), leaving the Namespace's actual served tier at whatever it was before the ambiguous edit landed — potentially a stale `baseline` from before a threat was priced up to `restricted`.
explanation: The code states "which one carries the party's tier is not the proposer's or the check's guess to make... `apply_tier_declaration()` refuses rather than rewriting one of them" — but this refusal is a refusal to *update*, not a fail-closed re-render to `isolated`. The stale pre-ambiguity tier keeps serving. This lets an adopter freeze a Namespace at a permissively low historical tier by introducing ambiguity right when a tightening would otherwise land, violating principle 6 (tightened by price, never escaped by procedural stalling) and principle 13 (disagreement resolved by open PR, not by indefinite unresolved ambiguity).
judge_reasoning:
The refusal-to-write behavior in `apply_tier_declaration()` is correct and must stay (it's the "could-not-look" principle from ADR-0020). The gap is on the read side: `cage-tier`'s MutatingPolicy currently reads *whatever single object the API server serves*, and since Kubernetes only stores one live Namespace object per name, "two documents in a manifest" collapses at apply-time to whichever one last applied cleanly — meaning the ambiguity is invisible to the webhook, which just sees a normal (possibly stale) tier label and serves it.

This is fixable without touching any prior resolution: principle 7 already establishes "an unknown or unlabelled tier fails closed to `isolated`... silence is not an exemption and it is not a refusal either; silence is the bottom rung." The loophole is that "ambiguous declaration" is a distinct unresolved state from "silence/unlabelled," and the code never said what the *serving* side does with it — only what the *proposer* does. Extending the fail-closed rule to cover ambiguity is a direct, non-contradictory application of the same principle, not a new exception. It doesn't conflict with the "refuses rather than rewriting one of them" rule (that's a proposer/write-path rule); it adds a serve/read-path rule that treats detected ambiguity the same as an unknown tier.

Concretely: the estate needs a mechanism (e.g., an admission/validating check, or `cage-tier` itself via a lookup across all governed-Namespace documents for that name at render/compose time, not just the live object) that detects multiple governed Namespace declarations for one name and marks the rendered tier as unknown → `isolated`, exactly mirroring the "two docs, one file" ambiguity-counting fix already made to the proposer's ambiguity guard. This closes the loophole using the existing fail-closed vocabulary rather than inventing a refusal.
judge_resolution_summary: The loophole exploited the fact that "refusal to rewrite an ambiguous declaration" (a proposer-side rule) left the previously-served tier live indefinitely, because nothing said what the render/serve path should do when ambiguity is present. The fix extends the already-established fail-closed rule for unknown/unlabelled tiers (principle 7) to explicitly cover detected ambiguity at render time, so an ambiguous Namespace renders `isolated` rather than continuing to serve its stale pre-ambiguity tier — closing the stalling loophole without altering the proposer's write-refusal behavior or any other resolved rule.
judge_proposed_revision:
Add to the "tier per Namespace" section (or as a follow-on to the "two governed Namespace documents is a question, not a first answer" note): 

Detected ambiguity in a Namespace's governed declaration (multiple governed-Namespace documents resolving to the same Namespace name, whether in one file or across the composed artefact) is an **unknown tier**, not a stale one. The same per-document ambiguity check that stops `apply_tier_declaration()` from writing also runs at compose/render time feeding `cage-tier`: if it fires, the rendered `namespaceObject` view carries no valid tier for that Namespace, and clause 7's existing rule applies verbatim — an unknown or unlabelled tier fails closed to `isolated`. This is enforced by extending the composed-artefact validation (the same signed-artefact pipeline that already renders the tier) to refuse to emit a determinate tier value when ambiguity is detected, so the served value is `isolated` rather than whatever tier happened to be live before the ambiguous edit landed. The proposer-side refusal to rewrite is unchanged; what changes is that the gap between "refuses to write" and "serves stale" is closed by treating ambiguity as a serving-time unknown, exactly as silence already is.

scenario: An on-call SRE, during a live incident, creates an emergency debug pod in a governed Namespace declared `isolated` to run `tcpdump`/network diagnostics against a service that's silently dropping packets. The pod claims a valid `policy-version` but its Namespace's `isolated` tier strips all egress/ingress, so the SRE cannot reach the affected service or an external log sink to export diagnostic data, prolonging a customer-facing outage that a five-minute packet capture could resolve.
explanation: Principle 2/6 says a workload is only ever "unable to run", never deliberately denied, and is caged tighter "until untenable" — but the practical effect for this SRE is functionally a denial of the one action (network diagnostics) needed to fix the outage. There is no emergency-break-glass conditional policy (principle 4) offered, and principle 5's "let the cage implement control" doesn't help when the very capability needed is network reach. The code offers no legitimate path except a policy PR under review (principle 13), which cannot happen fast enough during an active incident — yet performing that diagnostic action is clearly morally right (minimizing customer harm) and should not be effectively blocked by rigid tightening.
judge_reasoning:
The scenario is a classic gap the code's own doctrine anticipates and has a designated fix for: principle 4, "the first legitimate alternative to an exemption is conditional policy: you may do X if you meet conditions C, so anyone meeting C is treated identically." Nothing in the code currently defines such a conditional policy for incident response; that's an omission, not a structural conflict.

A break-glass conditional policy — e.g. a `cage-tier` conditional rule that grants a narrowly-scoped, time-boxed, audited loosening of egress/ingress (to a bounded diagnostic tool set, for a bounded duration) when a pod carries a claim such as `incident.acme.io/ticket-id` matching an active, independently-verifiable incident record, signed/attested by an on-call system — satisfies principle 4 exactly: it is a condition anyone on-call with an open incident can meet, not a named-workload carve-out (so it doesn't violate principle 3's exemption ban). It is priced (time-boxed, audited, auto-expiring, logged, narrower than full `baseline`) rather than an unconditional denial-bypass, consistent with principle 6 ("caged tighter until untenable... reached by the price, never a carve-out"). It does not violate tighten-only (principle 8) at the webhook level, because — like the floor mechanism (principle 11, "lowering the floor is priced, never refused") — this is a new declared/conditional widening *mechanism* on the Namespace/party level, governed by a signed, reviewed policy (principle 13: the policy itself goes through PR review once, not per-incident), not an ad hoc runtime carve-out for one workload. It's structurally identical to how the code already permits a platform-role party to declare `infra`, or an adopter to declare a floor: a pre-authorized, uniformly-applicable condition that changes the workload's placement on the ladder.

This does not conflict with any resolved case (there are none yet) and does not conflict with the stated principles once "conditional policy" is properly instantiated — it is literally the mechanism principle 4 names as legitimate for exactly this kind of situation.
judge_resolution_summary: The apparent overreach is resolved not by weakening `isolated` in general, but by adding the conditional-policy mechanism the doctrine already names as the legitimate first alternative to an exemption: a pre-authorized, uniformly-applicable, time-boxed, audited "incident break-glass" widening of network reach, triggered by a verifiable claim (an open, attested incident + on-call identity) rather than by any named workload, keeping the system exemption-free while giving the SRE a fast, principled path to run diagnostics.
judge_proposed_revision:
Add a new conditional-policy rung to the ladder specification (not a new tier, but a bounded, auditable modifier of tier-derived egress/ingress on an existing declared tier): 

"Incident break-glass: A pod in a governed Namespace may carry a claim `incident.acme.io/ticket-id` referencing an open, independently verified incident record (verified by a signed attestation from the incident-management system, e.g. PagerDuty/Opsgenie webhook-signed). When present and valid, `cage-netpol` widens egress/ingress for that pod only to a fixed, narrow, pre-approved diagnostic allowlist (e.g. named log-sink endpoints, and same-namespace service reach for packet capture) for a fixed maximum duration (e.g. 30 minutes), after which the widening auto-expires and the pod reverts to its Namespace's declared tier reach. The condition (valid open incident + role membership on the on-call rotation) is checked identically for any workload meeting it — this is a conditional policy under principle 4, not an exemption: it names no workload, only a verifiable state (open incident + on-call identity). Every grant is logged and surfaced in the truth surface. This policy ships and is amended only via the standard PR-under-review process (principle 13); it is not invoked ad hoc per-incident — only its *conditions* are met ad hoc."

This is implemented as an additional MutatingPolicy composed with (not replacing) `cage-tier`/`cage-netpol`, so tighten-only at admission is preserved: the base cage still writes the tightest baseline, and the break-glass policy is the one place explicitly authorized to widen a specific, bounded reach window, analogous to the floor-lowering pricing mechanism in principle 11.

scenario: A developer spins up a brand-new project Namespace and, before anyone gets around to writing the governance manifest, deploys a simple internal documentation-wiki pod with a valid policy-version claim, intending only to preview it for a team review meeting that afternoon. Because the Namespace is ungoverned, the pod is treated identically to a hostile or misconfigured workload and lands on `isolated` with all capabilities dropped and first-eviction priority, causing it to be evicted mid-demo when cluster pressure hits.
explanation: Per the "ungoverned Namespace renders isolated" rule (2026-09-04 flip) and principle 7 ("silence buys nothing anywhere... silence is the bottom rung"), an innocent administrative lag in labeling a Namespace — not any malicious or risky behavior — results in the same treatment as a bad actor. This overbroad definitional sweep (treating "unlabelled" identically to "adversarial") punishes ordinary, benign onboarding delay with production-impacting eviction, which is disproportionate to the actual risk of a documentation wiki preview.
judge_reasoning:
The scenario describes exactly the behavior the code was deliberately designed to produce: an ungoverned Namespace (no governance manifest yet) renders `isolated`, and a pod inside it is caged to the bottom rung including first-eviction priority — per principle 7 ("silence buys nothing... silence is the bottom rung") and the 2026-09-04 flip's explicit rationale.

The "problem" framing — that innocent administrative lag is treated identically to hostile behavior — is not an oversight; it is the stated design decision. The ADR history shows this was actively debated: the assistant's narrower alternative (some form of exception for legitimate-but-unlabeled cases) was proposed and explicitly overruled by the owner on 2026-09-02, who insisted nothing is ever denied for being "risky" vs "safe" — a workload is only ever caged tighter based on what it declares, never on an assessment of intent or benignness. Any fix here (e.g., a grace period, a "new namespace" leniency window, or judging the wiki pod as low-risk) would require:

1. Distinguishing workloads by perceived intent/risk rather than declared conditions — this is precisely what principle 3 bans as an "exemption," and what principle 4 requires instead be expressed as objective, uniformly-applied conditions.
2. Weakening the fail-closed default that principle 7 and the hard-won 2026-09-04 flip established, specifically to protect against exactly this kind of "it's just a small workload, surely it's fine" reasoning — the CoreDNS tripwire example shows this fail-closed behavior is load-bearing, not incidental.

A seemingly reasonable fix — "give new Namespaces a grace period before defaulting to isolated" — is itself just an unlabeled/silent state persisting longer, which directly contradicts "silence buys nothing anywhere... silence is the bottom rung" and reopens the loosening-not-implemented decision (loosening must be priced/argued, not defaulted).

The correct action under the existing code is already available and non-exceptional: the developer should label/govern the Namespace (or accept a floor/tier declaration) before deploying — that is the conditional-policy path (principle 4) already provided. The eviction is the cage doing exactly what it was built to do — an admission-time consequence of an unmet condition, not a deliberate denial, and "too expensive to run" is an accepted bottom rung (principle 6), not a bug.

This is a genuine tension between developer convenience/proportionality and the deliberately fail-closed security posture, already argued and decided by the owner. It cannot be resolved by better drafting without contradicting the settled 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-04 decisions.
judge_conflict_explanation: The scenario is the intended operation of the fail-closed rule ("ungoverned Namespace renders isolated," principle 7's "silence is the bottom rung"), which was explicitly deliberated and defended: the owner overruled a narrower/gentler alternative on 2026-09-02, insisting the system never judges a workload's apparent riskiness or benignness — only its declared conditions. Any revision to spare "innocent" onboarding delay (grace periods, risk-based leniency, low-stakes-workload carve-outs) would necessarily reintroduce exactly the kind of intent/context-based exception principle 3 bans, and would weaken the fail-closed default whose importance is illustrated by the CoreDNS tripwire example in the same ADR. The available fix is not a code revision but developer behavior: govern the Namespace (or set a floor) before deploying, per the existing conditional-policy path (principle 4). This is a real tension between proportionality/DX and deliberate fail-closed security design, already argued and settled by the owner, so it must be escalated rather than patched.

scenario: A platform engineer who does NOT hold the `platform` role, but is trusted by their team lead to temporarily manage a shared tools Namespace, declares it `infra` to gain the reduced dials appropriate for a genuinely low-risk internal CI-caching service, believing (correctly, as it turns out) that the workload poses no more risk than existing `infra` namespaces. Because their party artefact lacks the `platform` role label, the declaration silently renders `isolated` instead of erroring, and the CI cache service — now stripped of all egress — fails to pull dependencies, breaking every team's build pipeline overnight.
explanation: Principle 12 mandates that only a `platform`-role party's `infra` declaration lands, with any other party's declaration silently rendering `isolated` rather than raising an error or requesting review. This "silent renders `isolated`" behavior (rather than a rejected/flagged declaration prompting a role-grant PR per principle 13) causes a well-intentioned, low-risk operational decision to silently cascade into unrelated teams' broken builds, with no warning surfaced to the engineer — overreach in enforcing a role gate through silent mutation rather than any legible feedback.
judge_reasoning:
The core mechanism (non-platform `infra` declaration → renders `isolated`) is a deliberate, principled fail-closed behavior per principle 12, and is consistent with principles 2, 3, and 7 (no denial, no exemption, unlabelled/invalid input fails to the bottom rung). The actual harm in this case isn't that the mutation happened — that's correct behavior — it's that the mutation was *silent*: no legible signal was surfaced to the declarant explaining why their namespace tightened, leaving them to discover it only via a broken pipeline. That's a defect in observability/feedback, not in the enforcement rule itself.

We can add a non-blocking, non-refusing feedback mechanism: when a non-platform-role party's Namespace document declares `infra`, the render pipeline (or `verify-infra-declaration.sh`-style tripwire, or `tier_binding.py`) emits a visible warning/annotation on the composed evidence and in the PR/pipeline output — e.g. `posture.acme.io/tier-declared-vs-rendered` mismatch surfaced as a CI annotation — pointing the party at the role-grant PR process (principle 13). This is not a Deny, not an exemption, not a refusal, and does not change what tier is written (still tighten-only, still `isolated` for non-platform `infra` claims). It only adds legibility. This is consistent with every principle: the cage still self-enforces via mutation (1, 2), no carve-out is created (3), and disagreement is still routed to an open PR (13) rather than a favour.

This is a minimal, additive revision — not a change to the security semantics — so it doesn't conflict with any resolved case (none yet exist) or any stated principle.
judge_resolution_summary: The `infra`-declaration-by-non-platform-party behavior itself is correct and must remain unchanged (fail-closed to `isolated`, no exemption, no refusal), but the case reveals it currently ships with no legible feedback. The fix adds a non-blocking diagnostic signal at declaration/render time — surfaced in the same tier-binding check that already exists — telling the declarant what happened and directing them to the role-grant PR process, without weakening or exempting the enforcement itself.
judge_proposed_revision: Add to the ADR-0022 "infra is a declaration, not a selection" section: when `apply_tier_declaration`/the render pipeline observes a Namespace document declaring `posture.acme.io/tier: infra` from a party whose `party.yaml` lacks the `platform` role, it still renders `isolated` (unchanged, tighten-only, no refusal) — but it additionally emits a non-blocking, legible signal alongside the composed evidence: a `tier-declaration-mismatch` annotation/CI-check comment stating "declared `infra` by non-platform party X; rendered `isolated`; to raise, open a role-grant pull request." This surfaces in the same shift-left/tier-binding job that already reads `proposed_tier` vs. the governed label, so it costs no new enforcement path — only a diagnostic one, discoverable at PR/apply time rather than only via downstream pipeline breakage. This does not alter which tier is written, does not become a Deny, and does not constitute an exemption; it only fixes the muteness of the existing mutation so disagreement can be routed to the open PR process (principle 13) before workloads fail.
